opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I've learned from Jensen is that learning never stops, no matter how senior you are. He's running one of the most valuable companies in the world, and he still reads papers, asks very basic questions, and wants to understand things from first principles. When we present research to him, he doesn't just want the headline result. He'll ask, "Why does this work? What's the underlying principle? If we scale this up ten times, what happens?" That has pushed me to understand my own work more deeply, because you can't hide behind jargon with him.

Another thing is his habit of reasoning from the end state. He likes to imagine what the world will look like in five or ten years, and then work backward to what we need to build today. For example, with physical AI and world models, the question wasn't "what's the next incremental paper?" It was "if robots and autonomous machines are going to be everywhere, what foundational technology do they need?" That's part of how we got to building world foundation models like Cosmos. That kind of thinking changed how I choose research problems. I try to pick problems that matter for where the field is going, not just where it is now.

He's also very open about learning from mistakes. He talks about failure quite candidly. That gives people permission to try ambitious things. In research, most ideas don't work, so having a leader who treats failure as part of learning, rather than something to punish, really matters.

Finally, I'd say it's his intensity and curiosity together. He's genuinely excited about technology. When you see someone at that level still that curious, it reminds you that your own curiosity is the most valuable thing you have as a researcher. So I try to keep that beginner's mindset: keep asking questions, keep reading, keep building.

fable-5.1.text:
Jensen is probably the most curious person I've ever worked with, and that's the thing that rubbed off on me the most. He's a CEO running a company of tens of thousands of people, but he still reads papers, he still asks very detailed technical questions, and he's not afraid to say "I don't understand this, explain it to me." That was surprising to me at first. In a lot of organizations, the more senior you get, the more you feel you have to pretend you already know everything. Jensen does the opposite. He treats not knowing as the starting point, and he'll keep asking until he actually gets it, not just gets a summary.

The second thing is how he learns from first principles. When we were working on generative models for simulation, on what became Cosmos, he didn't want to hear "this is the standard approach." He wanted to know why the model is built this way, what breaks if you change it, where the data comes from, what the physical constraints are. He pushes you to go back to the fundamentals, and very often that process reveals that the thing everyone assumed was fixed is actually a choice. That changed how I run my own team. I try to ask the naive question more, because the naive question is usually the one that matters.

And the third thing is speed. Jensen learns fast because he's willing to be wrong in public. He'll make a prediction, be corrected, update, and move on, with no ego about it. For a researcher, that's a very healthy model. We're trained to be careful, to protect our conclusions. He showed me that you can be rigorous and still move quickly, if you're honest about what you know and what you don't. I'm still working on that part, to be honest, but he's a good example to have in front of you every day.

sol-6.1.text:
What I’ve learned from Jensen is to approach learning with curiosity and a willingness to go back to first principles. When you encounter something you don’t understand, don’t just accept the explanation—keep asking why until you can reason through it yourself.

That’s something I try to bring into my research: being comfortable saying, “I don’t know,” and then doing the work to understand. It also means being willing to change my mind when the evidence points in a different direction.
